title: 5,300-Year-Old Iceman Has Living Microbes on His Body!
summary:
Imagine finding a mummy frozen in ice for over 5,000 years. You'd think nothing could still be alive on it, right? Wrong! Scientists just discovered that Ötzi the Iceman, a famous frozen mummy found in the Alps, is carrying tiny living passengers. These are yeasts—microbes so small you need a microscope to see them. And guess what? They can still grow in a lab today!

Ötzi was discovered in 1991 in the Italian Alps. Since then, he's been kept super cold, at -6°C (21.2°F), to stop his body from rotting. But researchers recently found four types of yeast on his remains. They took samples and put them in a warm, cozy lab dish. To their surprise, the yeasts woke up and started growing! "These yeasts accompanied Ötzi over thousands of years while he was preserved in the ice," says scientist Albert Zink.

How did the yeasts survive so long? Scientists think Ötzi's body thawed and refroze several times, especially in the first 1,500 years after he died. This might have helped the yeasts hang on. The team also checked the soil, air, and water near the mummy to make sure the yeasts really came from Ötzi, not from the museum. They did!

But here's the scary part: if these microbes wake up, they could start eating away at Ötzi's body. That would be a disaster because Ötzi has taught us so much about life in the Copper Age. We know he wore leather clothes, had tattoos, and even ate a big fatty meal before he died. He carried a copper ax from far away. Patrick Hunt, an archaeologist at Stanford University, says Ötzi is "the most important archaeological-science finding of the 20th century." So, scientists are racing to understand these cold-loving microbes to keep the Iceman safe for future generations.
why_it_matters: This ancient mummy still has tiny life on it, showing that even after thousands of years, living things can survive—just like some germs in your fridge can come back when thawed, reminding us to handle old things with care.

background_read: Ötzi the Iceman (a 5,300-year-old mummy discovered in the Alps, a large mountain range in Europe) gave us rare clues about how people lived thousands of years ago.
He was found in 1991 by hikers on the border of Italy and Austria.
Today, scientists like Albert Zink (who leads the research team in Bolzano, Italy) keep him frozen to preserve his body.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ötzi the Iceman, a 5,300-year-old mummy, and scientists like Albert Zink.
WHAT: Living yeasts were discovered on his body, and they woke up in a lab.
WHERE: In a lab after sampling from Ötzi, who is kept at -6°C in the Italian Alps.
WHY: Because the body thawed and refroze, helping the yeasts survive, but now they could damage the valuable mummy.

perspectives.description: Scientists are thrilled because these live yeasts are a window into ancient times and how life can persist.
Those who preserve Ötzi worry that the microbes could eat the mummy and destroy important clues about history.
Researchers race to understand the microbes to stop them from damaging the Iceman while still learning from them.
